catalog_quote: 2.4 Word stress Word stress has not been systematically studied as yet, and phrase and sentence stress not at all. There is some evidence for the occurrence of the definitive accent on some noun phrases (see Hovdhaugen 1989: 23). The following comments on word stress are quite preliminary. The following rules will give the correct stress assignment for most Tokelauan words. (1) If there is a long vowel, it receives the main stress: 'pā, pa'kū, 'māhina, 'fānau. (2) Otherwise, the syllable containing the penultimate vowel is stressed: 'manu, ma'natu, ti'ute, ti'oa, hu'iga, fof'ou, te'kau, fe'kei, fi'fio. (3) In compound words and cases of full reduplication (see 3.4) both parts of the compound keep their normal stress. Note that the causative prefix faka- behaves like a compounding element in this respect. ki'ato+'tama, ki'ato+ma'tua; 'peka+'peka; 'faka+ma'natu; 'tai+ka'kahi, 'ta+'ika+'i…

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page scan we hold of Hooper 1993 p. 11 (p. 26), with p. 12 continuation; locator correct. (2) The deciding source is a 1993 syntax PhD whose stress section is self-declared preliminary, but nothing better exists: Glottolog has no phonology-type reference for toke1240; Sharples 1976 (downloaded, TOC + sec. 2.1 scanned) has no stress section; Hovdhaugen et al. 1989: 22 (nb.no index) and Simona 1986: xxxi (as quoted by Middleton 2024: 14, downloaded) give the same long-vowel-else-penult rules; Middleton's 2024 Auckland PhD still relies on these, so no later dedicated study is in evidence. The classification (weight-hedged: long vowel attracts stress anywhere, else syllable with penultimate vowel; author hedge 'most words') matches all three statements. (3) list of works to obtain is short and print-only; the one open item found (Middleton 2024) was downloaded and confirms. (4) Status ade

sources.quote: Index confirms the exact phrase on p. 22: 'In most words the stress falls on the next to last syllable:'; p. 22 also has 'the stressed vowel/syllable'; p. 23 has 'the last vowel of a ... is stressed ... (lengthened)' and 'definite' (the definitive-accent remark Hooper cites as Hovdhaugen 1989: 23). The word 'penultimate', 'mora', 'long vowel' do not occur on p. 22, so the long-vowel clause wording could not be recovered. Page text itself NOT fetched (geo-restricted).
sources.note: The only other grammar of Tokelauan with a phonology chapter; pp. 22-23 carry an independent stress statement ('In most words the stress falls on the next to last syllable:') plus the definitive-accent note Hooper 1993 cites; reading the full page would show how it treats long vowels (our 'unbounded' weight edge rests on Hooper's rule (1) alone).
